issues.explanation: For a 68-year-old married man whose index trauma was a life-threatening accident, 'kids crying' and 'physical affection such as hugs' are difficult to reconcile as principal trauma triggers given the rest of the profile. The memory, appraisal, threat, and coping items all center on bodily pain, fragmented accident memory, hypervigilance, self-blame, and safety behaviors, but do not provide a plausible bridge from an accident trauma to these interpersonal/child-related triggers.

In an accident case this would be possible, but here it appears disconnected enough to question whether it belongs to the same formulation.

vignette:
Arthur is a sixty-eight-year-old married man who has spent decades in public life, first as a local councilman and then as a state-level politician. He came to therapy at the urging of his wife, who had grown increasingly worried about his withdrawal from family gatherings and his refusal to attend any community events that required him to ride in a car. For the first few sessions, Arthur sat rigidly in the armchair, his hands gripping his knees, and spoke in clipped sentences. He had not driven a vehicle in over a year, and he could no longer tolerate being a passenger for more than a few blocks without feeling his chest tighten and his vision narrow.

The event that shattered Arthur’s sense of safety happened on a rainy November evening two years ago. He was driving home alone from a late committee meeting, his car the only one on a winding rural road. A pickup truck crossed the centre line and struck his sedan head-on. Arthur remembers the impact not as a continuous story but as a series of frozen frames: the headlights growing impossibly large, the sound of metal folding, the sensation of his chest being crushed against the steering wheel. He can describe each moment as if it were a photograph pinned to a wall, but when he tries to tell the whole story aloud he loses the thread, his sentences collapse, and he falls silent. What he cannot escape, even now, is the physical memory. Whenever the crash returns to his mind, he feels a sharp pressure in his ribs and a burning along his left arm, exactly where the seatbelt had torn into him. The pickup driver was found to be legally intoxicated, and Arthur spent three weeks in the hospital with multiple fractures and a punctured lung.

In the months that followed, Arthur became convinced that the crash had happened because of the sort of person he was. He had always prided himself on being careful, on weighing every decision twice before acting. But now he ruminated endlessly on what he must have done wrong. He blamed himself for taking that road, for not leaving the meeting earlier, for not seeing the headlights sooner. He would lie awake at night and replay the sequence, searching for the moment where his own failure had sealed the outcome. His wife would find him at three in the morning, sitting up in bed, listening. Silence had become unbearable. An unusual quiet in the house, or even a pause in conversation, made him certain that something dangerous was about to happen. He began to wake repeatedly during the night to check that the doors were locked, that the windows were closed, that nothing was out of place. By dawn he was exhausted, and during the day he could not concentrate on the policy briefs and constituent letters that had once been his daily rhythm.

Arthur’s world shrank. He stopped driving entirely, and he avoided being a passenger whenever possible. If a meeting could not be moved to his home, he cancelled it. He told himself that he was being prudent, that the roads were unsafe, that other drivers were reckless. But he also felt that people could see what had happened to him just by looking at him. He was certain that his colleagues and his wife’s friends could read the crash in his face, in the way he flinched at the sound of a car horn, in the hesitation before he crossed a parking lot. He began to avoid public events, fearing that someone would ask him why he no longer drove, and that he would have to explain. The smell of alcohol, even from a single beer at a dinner party, sent a jolt through him that he could not disguise. He would excuse himself and stand in the kitchen until the feeling passed.

His marriage suffered. His wife, who had been his closest confidante, grew frustrated by his refusals and his silences. He could see the hurt in her eyes when he declined to accompany her to their granddaughter’s school play because it would require a forty-minute drive. He wanted to explain, but the words would not come. What frightened him most was the thought that this was permanent, that he had become someone who could not be fixed. He came to therapy not because he believed it would help, but because his wife had said she could not watch him disappear any longer. He sat in the chair, his hands still gripping his knees, and said quietly that he was tired of being afraid.
